problem_motivation.content: Particles need to be removed from the collection environment and placed into a precision-measurement environment.
problem_motivation.evidence_span:
To completely remove the particle from the environment
where it is collected and move it into an environment opti-
mized for precision measurements, we describe our process
for transferring particles between two ion traps (Section VI).

problem_motivation.content: High-quality characterization data require waiting days for stabilization after electrospray collection.
problem_motivation.evidence_span:
While we have established that high quality data like that
shown in Fig. 4 is possible to obtain, we have found that to do
so it is necessary to wait a substantial amount of time (∼days)
for peak amplitudes and positions to stabilize.

problem_motivation.content: Transfer to a separate analysis trap is needed because collection creates slowly decaying stray fields and because a better vacuum and specialized measurements are desired.
problem_motivation.evidence_span:
There are several reasons to transfer a particle from a col-
lection trap to a different analysis trap for additional measure-
ments... First,
as we emphasized in the previous section, charged parti-
cle collection can create stray electric fields that decay very
slowly with time and can have a deleterious effect on mea-
surements... Particle transfer allows the
particle to be moved out of the low vacuum collection cham-
ber and into a chamber capable of much better vacuum31.
The separate analysis trap and chamber can be configured and op-
timized for operations that are not practical in the collection
chamber

problem_motivation.content: High-vacuum measurements require active cooling because gas friction becomes negligible while heating sources remain.
problem_motivation.evidence_span:
High vacuum measurements necessitate
an instrumental mechanism to cool the particle, since fric-
tion from background gases becomes negligible, and heating
mechanisms (like those that impacted the data in Section V)
are inevitably present.

prior_approach.content: Previous work measured mass-related phenomena of levitated nanoparticles via trap oscillation and Q/M methods.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
Mass (M) for particles confined in ion (Paul) traps is de-
termined from the charge to mass ratio (Q/M) which in turn
is inferred from particle oscillation frequencies (νx,νy,νz) in
the trap.

prior_approach.content: Earlier studies reported extremely high quality factors and frequency stability in ultrahigh vacuum ion traps.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
Recently, quality factors in excess of 1010 have
been reported for particles oscillating in ion traps in an ultra-
high vacuum (pressure p = 7 × 10−11 mbar) environment11.
In these experiments, Allan deviation for the oscillation fre-
quency reached a minimum of 2 × 10−6, suggesting that a
similar precision is possible for measurements of Q/M and
M in high vacuum.

prior_approach.content: The authors had previously reported a two-trap transfer technique using perpendicular single-pair conical electrodes.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
We have previously reported on this technique14 using two
traps, each consisting of a single pair of coaxial conically
shaped electrodes (Fig. 1a) oriented on perpendicular axes.

prior_approach.content: The transfer operation had been previously described by the authors.
prior_approach.evidence_span: an operation we have previously described14.

prior_approach.content: Biconal trap designs similar to the chosen analysis trap were previously used for single-ion trapping and small-particle analysis.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
One highly attractive analysis trap design is the "biconal
trap", illustrated in Fig. 1c and d, which is similar to designs
previously used for single ion trapping15,16 and for small par-
ticle analysis33.

prior_approach.content: The authors had previously described methods for long-term particle stability below 1e-6 Torr.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
We have previously described our techniques for obtaining
long term particle stability for measurements at p below 10−6
Torr35.

prior_approach.content: The setup uses avalanche photodetectors and a knife-edge beam splitter to sense 3D particle motion.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
We employ a knife edge beam splitter and two small
arrays of avalanche photodetectors39 to sense motion along
all three axes of a particle confined in an ion trap (Fig. 9).

prior_approach.content: Parametric feedback cooling is used to stabilize the particle in high vacuum.
prior_approach.evidence_span:
We use parametric feedback cooling (Fig. 10) to stabilize the
particle in high vacuum35.

prior_limitation.content: The simple aperture-flow model neglects fluid dynamics, particle charge effects, and mass loss from evaporation or fission.
prior_limitation.evidence_span:
This model has obvious deficiencies: fluid dynamics and
the effects of charge on the particles are neglected. Also, the
complexities of mass loss of the particles as liquid evaporates
or droplets fission are not considered.

prior_limitation.content: Simple cooling gives oscillation amplitudes that are too small for best frequency measurements and often fails below 1e-7 Torr because PLL tracking is lost.
prior_limitation.evidence_span:
However, measure-
ments of trap oscillation frequencies (from which one can de-
duce Q/M) are best performed when the oscillation ampli-
tudes are not too small. We have also found that the simple
cooling algorithm often fails at p ≤10−7 Torr, when the am-
plitude of oscillations can become so small that the PLL is
unable to track the signal. When this happens, the particle is
not lost, but Q/M measurements are compromised.

rejected_alternative.content: Unlike single-cone traps, the work favors symmetric biconal traps because they avoid odd expansion terms and preserve broad access.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span:
Unlike the case for single cone traps, bi-
conal trap potentials are symmetric, so odd terms in the poly-
nomial expansion around the minimum are absent. Biconal
traps maintain ease of access for measurements at all angles
in the plane of symmetry

causal_claim.content: Electrospray-based injection deposits charged particles on nearby electrodes and causes excess noise that decays over days.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
These
measurements also provide insight into the excess noise that
originates from charge on the surfaces of trap electrodes13:
particle injection techniques like electrospray–which deliver
charged particles not only to the trap, but also deposit them on
the nearby electrodes–create excess noise that slowly decays
(over days) until thermal equilibrium is reached.

causal_claim.content: The symmetric trap geometry provides nearly full optical access and roughly doubles achievable center electric fields.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
In this configuration there is almost
360◦access for optics and beams in the symmetry plane, and
the symmetric design means that the achievable electric field
strengths at the trap center (for example, for coupling to parti-
cle electric dipoles17) are approximately double those possible
with our previous design.

causal_claim.content: Gas flow through the aperture accelerates electrosprayed particles to high velocities, making stopping distance important.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Since
particles created by electrospray will be accelerated to high
velocities by this flow, it is important to approximate the nec-
essary distance between the aperture and the trap to ensure
that particles are slowed and come to a stop prior to capture.

causal_claim.content: Applying AC together with oppositely signed DC expands the basin of attraction and increases charged-particle collection rate.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Applying Vac and a simultaneous Vdc with polar-
ity opposite to the particle charge creates a greatly expanded
basin of attraction for the trap that increases the rate of collec-
tion of charged particles passing by (Fig. 1b).

causal_claim.content: Charged droplets reaching the trap can cause excess surface charge on the electrodes.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
As will be discussed further in the following section,
charged droplets reaching the trap during electrospraying can
lead to excess surface charge on the electrodes.

causal_claim.content: Opening the gate valve only after a stable plume is established reduces charge deposition issues from electrospray collection.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Consequently,
we open the gate valve that separates the emission source from
the trap (Fig. 2a) only after a stable plume of the particle sus-
pension has been established.

causal_claim.content: Liquid droplets rapidly lose mass and are quickly ejected from the trap, unlike solid particles.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Almost all of these are liquid droplets that
rapidly lose mass and are quickly (seconds) ejected from the
trap. Solid particles are collected much less frequently

causal_claim.content: Charge deposited on trap electrodes during electrospray creates electric fields that decay slowly over time.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
When particles
are collected during the electrospray process, charged parti-
cles inevitably also land on the trap electrodes. Accumulation
of these charges leads to electric fields, primarily along the z-
axis, that slowly decay with time.

causal_claim.content: These time-varying stray fields shift peak positions and inflate amplitudes beyond thermal-equilibrium values.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Over a few days, the necessary nulling potential rises
until |Vdc| < 0.5 V. During this time, peak positions shift, and
their amplitudes, especially for motion along the z-axis, sig-
nificantly exceed the values predicted from the assumption
that the particle is in thermal equilibrium.

causal_claim.content: The authors infer that the actual Au particle size spread likely exceeds the manufacturer's specification.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
From this data, we believe it is likely that the
actual spread of the sizes of the Au particles exceeds the man-
ufacturer’s specifications.

causal_claim.content: Particle transfer enables removal from the low-vacuum chamber into a better-vacuum analysis chamber and allows operations impractical in the collection chamber.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Particle transfer allows the
particle to be moved out of the low vacuum collection cham-
ber and into a chamber capable of much better vacuum31. The
separate analysis trap and chamber can be configured and op-
timized for operations that are not practical in the collection
chamber, such as exposure to an electron beam or deposition
of trapped particles onto a substrate32.

causal_claim.content: Machining a slot intentionally breaks rotational symmetry so the three motional axes have distinct frequencies.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
The slot
intensionally breaks the rotational symmetry of the traps, so
that motion in the directions parallel and perpendicular to the
slots have different frequencies.

causal_claim.content: Viewing at 45 degrees to the slot allows motion along all three trap axes to be distinguished.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
When the trap is viewed from
a 45◦angle from the slot direction, motion along all three trap
axes can be distinguished and analyzed (Fig. 6b-d).

causal_claim.content: Photodetectors provide faster response than cameras, benefiting position detection and rapid rotation measurements.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Compared to the camera technique described in Section 2,
the photodetectors have a faster response time, which is rel-
evant both for position detection and for rapid measurements
of particle rotation17.

causal_claim.content: The slotted-trap geometry produces three distinct motional frequencies, requiring three PLLs for full control.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
In trap designs with a slot geometry, as in Fig. 6, motion
within the trap has three distinct frequencies. To control mo-
tion in all three frequencies we employ three phase locked
loops (PLLs) that track motion in all directions of the ion trap.

causal_claim.content: Thermostatic control cools above an upper amplitude threshold, heats below a lower threshold, and suppresses feedback in between.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
Our implementation maintains
oscillation amplitudes within a band: above an upper limit,
feedback provides cooling, while below a lower limit, feed-
back heats the particle. All feedback is suppressed within the
range of the lower and upper bands.

causal_claim.content: Long-term amplitude variations of the high-voltage amplifier can affect Q/M through Vac, so Vac is measured directly and corrected.
causal_claim.evidence_span:
As can be seen from Eq. 10, both Ω and Vac contribute to
Q/M... Vac, how-
ever, is the output of a high voltage amplifier that has signif-
icant (∼0.1%) long term amplitude variations, probably due
to temperature fluctuations. To account for these fluctuations,
we measure the amplitude with a lock-in amplifier

causal_claim.content: Imaging trapped particles' thermal motion enables fast estimation of particle mass and size, useful when collected material is uncertain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Imaging of thermal motion of trapped particles is a fast way to characterize the mass and size of particles, which is useful in situations where there is uncertainty in what is collected (possible particle aggregation, for example).

causal_claim.content: Being able to leave particles unilluminated and without feedback may benefit studies where light or heating alters material properties.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The ability to do this may have important applications for investigations of levitated materials where light or thermal effects have an effect on material properties.

causal_claim.content: Charges from pumps or other sources would create unwanted electric fields and gradients that disturb measurements.
causal_claim.evidence_span: to prevent unwanted electric fields and gradients from affecting trap measurements.

causal_claim.content: High-vacuum particle stabilization and precision measurement will enable new ways to probe nanoscale materials.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Particle stabilization and precision measurements in high vacuum will open the door to new probes of nanoscale materials.

causal_claim.content: The reported Q/M precision should permit measurements of sub-monolayer surface accumulation on micron-scale particles in UHV.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the precision we report of δ(Q/M)/⟨Q/M⟩≃10−5 should allow measurements of sub-monolayer surface accumulations on micron-scale particles in UHV

mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
These
measurements also provide insight into the excess noise that
originates from charge on the surfaces of trap electrodes13:
particle injection techniques like electrospray–which deliver
charged particles not only to the trap, but also deposit them on
the nearby electrodes–create excess noise

mechanism_principle.content: The improved field strength follows from the symmetric design of the trap.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
the symmetric design means that the achievable electric field
strengths at the trap center (for example, for coupling to parti-
cle electric dipoles17) are approximately double those possible
with our previous design

mechanism_principle.content: Au slows more slowly because its greater density/inertia reduces deceleration.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span:
with the Au particle sig-
nificantly slower, due to its greater inertia

hypothesis_statement.content: The developed instrumentation and techniques are intended to enable high-stability precision measurements in high vacuum.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
We describe below the experimental instrumentation and
techniques that we have developed that are optimized for high-
stability precision measurements of particles confined in ion
traps in high vacuum (10−8 ≤p ≤10−5 Torr).

hypothesis_statement.content: Three PLLs and thermostatic control should maintain amplitudes optimal for frequency and Q/M measurements.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
In Section VII, we discuss
a method for using three phase locked loops (PLLs) to track
trapped particle motion along all three axes of confinement.
Using these PLL outputs, we implement thermostatic control
of particle motion in order to maintain amplitudes that are
optimal for measuring motional frequencies and determining
Q/M.

hypothesis_statement.content: Despite its simplifications, the model should still give roughly correct particle velocities and stopping distances.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
We nonetheless expect
that the model provides crude estimates of typical particle ve-
locities and stopping distances that are not too far off.

hypothesis_statement.content: Rapid imaging of thermal motion can provide more extensive post-capture particle characterization.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
To obtain more extensive data on the particle soon after it is
collected, we have developed a technique that performs rapid
imaging12 on the particle to observe thermal motion in the
trap.

hypothesis_statement.content: Adding thermostatic control should solve the low-amplitude tracking problem in the cooling algorithm.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
To remedy this problem, we have added thermostatic con-
trol to our cooling algorithm (Fig. 10).

hypothesis_statement.content: The noise is primarily due to low-frequency fluctuations in DC electric fields from charge on the trap electrodes, especially along z.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span:
These observations are
consistent with the hypothesis that low frequency fluctuations
in the dc electric fields associated with charge on the trap elec-
trodes are the primary source of noise, and that fields along the
trap z axis have the largest magnitudes.

hypothesis_statement.content: The transfer technique could be extended to move a particle among multiple specialized traps.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This technique could in principle be extended to transferring a particle between several traps, each optimized for specific tasks or measurements.

hypothesis_statement.content: The precision-measurement methods are expected to work also in the UHV regime.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Although our techniques for precision measurements have been developed and proven at p ≥10−8 Torr, we expect that they will also be applicable in the ultra high vacuum (UHV) regime.

hypothesis_statement.content: Combining these methods with precision rotation and controlled deposition may enable growth and characterization of new levitated materials.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: These techniques, in combination with precision rotation17 and controlled deposition of levitated particles32, may also enable the growth and characterization of new materials developed in the levitated environment.

evidence_result.content: The study shows transfer is also possible into a symmetric two-pair coaxial conical electrode trap.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
We show that it is also possible to transfer into a symmetric ar-
rangement of two coaxial conical electrode pairs facing each
other (Fig. 1c,d), a trap geometry similar to those adopted
by several groups2,15,16.

evidence_result.content: The stabilization methods allowed locked particle motion for over a month.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
Using these techniques, we have been able to lock and
stabilize particle motion for over a month.

evidence_result.content: Q/M precision reached about 1e-5 for 10-minute averages at around 1e-8 Torr.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
We report a peak precision
of δ(Q/M)/⟨Q/M⟩∼= 10−5 for data averaged over ten minute
periods.

evidence_result.content: Numerical integration indicates Au particles decelerate slowly and need over 20 cm to stop.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
As shown in Fig. 3, the particles accelerate
to a velocity somewhat less than u0, with the Au particle sig-
nificantly slower, due to its greater inertia. While particle ac-
celeration occurs near the aperture, deceleration occurs much
more slowly, due to the much lower gas pressure in the col-
lection chamber when y/r0 ≫1 (Fig. 3, inset). In this regime,
we assume that the residual gas is at rest relative to the par-
ticle. Again, velocity change is less rapid for the denser Au
particle, which takes over 20 cm to come to rest.

evidence_result.content: Observed y and z spectral peaks match expectations, and fitted mass and diameter are within 10% of manufacturer values.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
That is exactly what is seen in
Fig. 4, and fits to the spectra produce values of M and D
within 10% of the values expected from the manufacturer’s
specifications28 for the nanosphere dimensions.

evidence_result.content: Rapid characterization distinguishes dense Au particles from lower-density polystyrene particles of similar mass and brightness.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
From the data, it is easy
to distinguish the high density Au particles from much lower
density polystyrene nanospheres with comparable mass and
brightness.

evidence_result.content: Even rapid measurements are sufficient to identify contaminants and particle aggregates.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
Although the best data can only be obtained a day or so
after collection, rapid (<1 hour) measurements are still pos-
sible and are valuable for quick characterization of collected
particles: first, to distinguish high density (like Au) and much
lower density organic contaminant particles. Secondly, aggre-
gates of >1 particle will be distinguishable from single par-
ticles, since even quick data collection is unlikely to lead to
mass errors exceeding 100%.

evidence_result.content: The authors successfully demonstrated particle transfer into the analysis trap and back again.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
To demonstrate transfer, we collected a 600 nm polystyrene
particle with Q/M ≃7 C·kg−1 in the collection trap... By reversing the order of the process steps, we are
also able to return the particle from the analysis trap back to
its original position in the collection chamber.

evidence_result.content: The simplest cooling algorithm was enough for week-scale stability and 1-10 K center-of-mass temperatures at up to 1e-6 Torr.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
The simplest possible cooling algorithm, where the para-
metric feedback phase is set for maximum cooling, has proven
adequate for long term stability (>∼weeks), with center of mass
temperatures of 1-10 K at p ≤10−6 Torr.

evidence_result.content: Thermostatic control operated successfully from 1e-8 to 1e-5 Torr and kept PLLs locked for weeks at the lowest pressures.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
We
set the values for the band limits to maintain an amplitude
of ∼2 µm for motion along each of the three axes... We
have operated the thermostatic control algorithm successfully
in the range 10−8 ≤p ≤10−5 Torr. At the lowest pressures,
measurements can remain stable–all the PLLs are locked to
the particle motion–for several weeks.

evidence_result.content: A single charge-loss event was resolved, allowing the particle mass to be determined as 7.1±0.25×10^-17 kg.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
Q/M data is shown in Fig. 12a near a time when Q changes
by a single elementary charge... The single discharge event allows the mass
to be determined: M = 7.1±0.25×10−17 kg.

evidence_result.content: Q/M derived from νz is noisier than from νx or νy, so the authors use qx+qy for Q/M determination.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
Two facts about the data are important: first, data derived
from νz has significantly more noise than the other two modes
of oscillation. Consequently, we exclusively use qx +qy to de-
termine Q/M

evidence_result.content: The behavior of γ supports the interpretation that DC-field effects diminish at higher trap frequencies.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
This idea is corrobo-
rated by the behavior of γ shown in Fig. 12c, which rapidly
declines to < 10−4 when the trap frequencies used to deter-
mine it are at their highest values.

evidence_result.content: For averaging times longer than about 10 minutes, relative Q/M precision is below 1e-5.
evidence_result.evidence_span:
For averaging times greater than ∼10
minutes, δ(Q/M)/⟨Q/M⟩< 10−5.

evidence_result.content: Thermal-motion imaging yielded insight into non-thermal noise affecting ion traps exposed to charged particles.
evidence_result.evidence_span: This data has also provided insight into non-thermal noise that is relevant when ion traps are exposed to charged particles.

evidence_result.content: After transfer and pumping to high vacuum, particles remained trapped for up to 24 hours even with feedback and illumination turned off.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Interestingly, we have found that once a particle has been transferred to an analysis trap and pumped to high vacuum, all feedback control can be interrupted and illumination of the particle entirely turned off for periods of up to 24 hours without particle loss from the trap.

constraint.content: Because Au is highly absorptive, measurements must use very low illumination power density.
constraint.evidence_span:
Au, like many other materials of interest, is highly
absorptive, so our measurements are performed using an illu-
mination of only 1000 W·m−2 at 532 nm.

constraint.content: The pinhole aperture must be large enough to avoid clogging and pass particles, yet keep trap pressure below about 1 Torr to avoid corona discharge.
constraint.evidence_span:
The inner diameter of the pinhole aperture that separates the
electrospray emitter from the trap vacuum chamber should be
large enough to avoid clogging and admit as many particles
as possible. However, the pressure in the trap region must be
lower than ∼1 Torr to prevent corona discharge arising from
the high voltages (Vac ≃300 V) on the trap electrodes.

constraint.content: Good thermal-motion spectra require low pressure, adjusted trap frequency below 500 Hz, and no laser-heating effect.
constraint.evidence_span:
While particles are collected at p ∼=700 mTorr, optimal
data for spectra for particles of sub-µm dimensions is ob-
tained when p =10-30 mTorr... Because Q/M of the particles–and thus their oscillation
frequencies–can vary substantially, it is necessary to adjust
Ωso that both y and z peaks are found at <500 Hz... Finally, data must be taken in a regime when
changes in laser power have no effect on the data, ensuring
that the particles are in thermal equilibrium with background
gas at T ∼=293 K.

constraint.content: To avoid evaporation of highly absorptive Au, illumination must remain well below the level causing significant heating.
constraint.evidence_span:
Because Au is highly absorptive, illumination power must
be well below that where significant evaporation can oc-
cur: we use a 532 nm laser with a power density of ≃1000
W·m−2.

constraint.content: The achieved precision is not enough to determine the exact charge of the shown particle in one step, though it would suffice for particles with n≤300.
constraint.evidence_span:
Thus, the precision of δ(Q/M)/⟨Q/M⟩≃10−5 is insufficient
to determine exactly the charge on the object in Fig. 12a, but
a single step determination of the exact charge would be pos-
sible for n ≤300.

constraint.content: For UHV application, the trap region must be shielded from charges from pumps and other ion/electron sources.
constraint.evidence_span: However, it will be necessary to carefully shield the trap neighborhood from charges emanating from ion pumps or other sources of ions and electrons

contradiction.content: Despite using two orders of magnitude lower illumination than prior silica work, the achieved precision is only five times worse.
contradiction.evidence_span:
This power den-
sity is two orders of magnitude less than that used on silica
nanospheres in Ref. 11, Nevertheless, the precision reported
in those results is only a factor of five better than what we
have obtained for particles of similar dimensions.

contradiction.content: The spread in measured Au nanosphere data is larger than the manufacturer's stated specifications.
contradiction.evidence_span:
The spread of our data for Au nanospheres substan-
tially exceeds that quoted in the manufacturer’s specifica-
tions.

problem_motivation.content: A key motivation is to move particles out of the electrospray/collection environment and into a separate precision-analysis environment, because collection can generate slowly decaying stray electric fields that degrade measurements, the collection chamber has poorer vacuum, and the analysis setup can be optimized for specialized measurements.
evidence_spans: To completely remove the particle from the environment where it is collected and move it into an environment optimized for precision measurements, we describe our process for transferring particles between two ion traps (Section VI).

There are several reasons to transfer a particle from a collection trap to a different analysis trap for additional measurements... First, as we emphasized in the previous section, charged particle collection can create stray electric fields that decay very slowly with time and can have a deleterious effect on measurements... Particle transfer allows the particle to be moved out of the low vacuum collection chamber and into a chamber capable of much better vacuum31. The separate analysis trap and chamber can be configured and optimized for operations that are not practical in the collection chamber

problem_motivation.content: Another motivation is that obtaining high-quality characterization data in the collection setup otherwise requires waiting days for peak amplitudes and positions to stabilize, motivating transfer to a cleaner measurement environment.
evidence_spans: While we have established that high quality data like that shown in Fig. 4 is possible to obtain, we have found that to do so it is necessary to wait a substantial amount of time (∼days) for peak amplitudes and positions to stabilize.

problem_motivation.content: For high-vacuum precision measurements, the system also needs an active cooling mechanism, because gas damping becomes negligible in high vacuum while heating sources remain.
evidence_spans: High vacuum measurements necessitate an instrumental mechanism to cool the particle, since friction from background gases becomes negligible, and heating mechanisms (like those that impacted the data in Section V) are inevitably present.

prior_approach.content: Prior work determined the mass of particles confined in Paul/ion traps from the charge-to-mass ratio (Q/M), inferred from the particle’s trap oscillation frequencies; related studies in ultrahigh vacuum also reported extremely high quality factors (>10^10) and very low Allan deviation (~2 × 10^-6), indicating high precision for Q/M and mass measurements.
evidence_spans:
Mass (M) for particles confined in ion (Paul) traps is de-
termined from the charge to mass ratio (Q/M) which in turn
is inferred from particle oscillation frequencies (νx,νy,νz) in
the trap.

Recently, quality factors in excess of 1010 have
been reported for particles oscillating in ion traps in an ultra-
high vacuum (pressure p = 7 × 10−11 mbar) environment11.
In these experiments, Allan deviation for the oscillation fre-
quency reached a minimum of 2 × 10−6, suggesting that a
similar precision is possible for measurements of Q/M and
M in high vacuum.

prior_limitation.content: Prior approaches were limited by an oversimplified aperture-flow/cooling treatment: the simple aperture-flow model neglected important physics such as fluid dynamics, particle charge effects, and particle mass loss from evaporation or droplet fission, while simple cooling could drive oscillation amplitudes too low for accurate frequency (and thus Q/M) measurements and often failed below about 1e-7 Torr because PLL tracking was lost.
evidence_spans: This model has obvious deficiencies: fluid dynamics and the effects of charge on the particles are neglected. Also, the complexities of mass loss of the particles as liquid evaporates or droplets fission are not considered.

However, measurements of trap oscillation frequencies (from which one can deduce Q/M) are best performed when the oscillation amplitudes are not too small. We have also found that the simple cooling algorithm often fails at p ≤10−7 Torr, when the amplitude of oscillations can become so small that the PLL is unable to track the signal. When this happens, the particle is not lost, but Q/M measurements are compromised.

rejected_alternative.content: Single-cone traps were rejected in favor of symmetric biconal traps, because biconal traps eliminate odd terms in the polynomial expansion around the minimum and still provide easy measurement access at all angles in the plane of symmetry.
evidence_spans:
Unlike the case for single cone traps, bi-
conal trap potentials are symmetric, so odd terms in the poly-
nomial expansion around the minimum are absent. Biconal
traps maintain ease of access for measurements at all angles
in the plane of symmetry

causal_claim.content: During electrospray-based particle injection, charged droplets/particles can land on nearby trap electrodes, depositing surface charge that creates stray electric fields and excess noise; these fields/noise decay only slowly over days as the system returns toward thermal equilibrium.
evidence_spans: These measurements also provide insight into the excess noise that originates from charge on the surfaces of trap electrodes13: particle injection techniques like electrospray–which deliver charged particles not only to the trap, but also deposit them on the nearby electrodes–create excess noise that slowly decays (over days) until thermal equilibrium is reached.
As will be discussed further in the following section, charged droplets reaching the trap during electrospraying can lead to excess surface charge on the electrodes.

When particles are collected during the electrospray process, charged particles inevitably also land on the trap electrodes. Accumulation of these charges leads to electric fields, primarily along the z-axis, that slowly decay with time.

causal_claim.content: These slowly decaying, time-varying stray fields from electrospray-deposited charge shift motional peak positions and increase amplitudes beyond values expected at thermal equilibrium.
evidence_spans: Over a few days, the necessary nulling potential rises until |Vdc| < 0.5 V. During this time, peak positions shift, and their amplitudes, especially for motion along the z-axis, significantly exceed the values predicted from the assumption that the particle is in thermal equilibrium.

When particles are collected during the electrospray process, charged particles inevitably also land on the trap electrodes. Accumulation of these charges leads to electric fields, primarily along the z-axis, that slowly decay with time.

causal_claim.content: Gas flow through the aperture accelerates electrosprayed particles to high velocities, so sufficient distance between the aperture and trap is needed for the particles to slow and stop before capture.
evidence_spans: Since particles created by electrospray will be accelerated to high velocities by this flow, it is important to approximate the necessary distance between the aperture and the trap to ensure that particles are slowed and come to a stop prior to capture.

causal_claim.content: Applying an AC trapping voltage together with a DC bias of opposite polarity to the particle charge greatly expands the trap’s basin of attraction and increases the collection rate of passing charged particles.
evidence_spans: Applying Vac and a simultaneous Vdc with polarity opposite to the particle charge creates a greatly expanded basin of attraction for the trap that increases the rate of collection of charged particles passing by (Fig. 1b).

causal_claim.content: To reduce electrode charging from electrospray collection, the gate valve to the trap is opened only after a stable electrospray plume has been established.
evidence_spans: Consequently, we open the gate valve that separates the emission source from the trap (Fig. 2a) only after a stable plume of the particle suspension has been established.

causal_claim.content: Liquid droplets collected from electrospray rapidly lose mass and are ejected from the trap within seconds, unlike solid particles.
evidence_spans: Almost all of these are liquid droplets that rapidly lose mass and are quickly (seconds) ejected from the trap. Solid particles are collected much less frequently

causal_claim.content: The authors infer from their data that the actual size distribution of the Au particles is broader than the manufacturer's specification.
evidence_spans: From this data, we believe it is likely that the actual spread of the sizes of the Au particles exceeds the manufacturer’s specifications.

causal_claim.content: Machining a slot into the trap intentionally breaks rotational symmetry, causing motion along different axes to have distinct frequencies; in the slotted geometry this yields three distinct motional frequencies, so three PLLs are used for full control.
evidence_spans: The slot intensionally breaks the rotational symmetry of the traps, so that motion in the directions parallel and perpendicular to the slots have different frequencies.

In trap designs with a slot geometry, as in Fig. 6, motion within the trap has three distinct frequencies. To control motion in all three frequencies we employ three phase locked loops (PLLs) that track motion in all directions of the ion trap.

causal_claim.content: Long-term amplitude drift of the high-voltage amplifier changes Vac and therefore affects inferred Q/M, so Vac is measured directly and corrected.
evidence_spans: As can be seen from Eq. 10, both Ω and Vac contribute to Q/M... Vac, however, is the output of a high voltage amplifier that has significant (∼0.1%) long term amplitude variations, probably due to temperature fluctuations. To account for these fluctuations, we measure the amplitude with a lock-in amplifier

causal_claim.content: Imaging the thermal motion of trapped particles provides a fast estimate of particle mass and size, which is useful when the identity or aggregation state of collected material is uncertain.
evidence_spans: Imaging of thermal motion of trapped particles is a fast way to characterize the mass and size of particles, which is useful in situations where there is uncertainty in what is collected (possible particle aggregation, for example).

causal_claim.content: Leaving trapped particles unilluminated and without feedback may be advantageous for studies in which light exposure or heating alters material properties.
evidence_spans: The ability to do this may have important applications for investigations of levitated materials where light or thermal effects have an effect on material properties.

causal_claim.content: Unwanted charge from pumps or other sources would generate electric fields and gradients that disturb trap measurements, motivating efforts to prevent such charging.
evidence_spans: to prevent unwanted electric fields and gradients from affecting trap measurements.

causal_claim.content: Stabilizing particles and performing precision measurements in high vacuum will enable new probes of nanoscale materials.
evidence_spans: Particle stabilization and precision measurements in high vacuum will open the door to new probes of nanoscale materials.

causal_claim.content: The achieved precision in Q/M is sufficient to enable measurements of sub-monolayer surface accumulation on micron-scale particles in ultrahigh vacuum.
evidence_spans: the precision we report of δ(Q/M)/⟨Q/M⟩≃10−5 should allow measurements of sub-monolayer surface accumulations on micron-scale particles in UHV

mechanism_principle.content: Excess noise arises because electrospray deposition leaves charge on nearby trap-electrode surfaces, and this accumulated surface charge creates the noise.
evidence_spans: These measurements also provide insight into the excess noise that originates from charge on the surfaces of trap electrodes13: particle injection techniques like electrospray–which deliver charged particles not only to the trap, but also deposit them on the nearby electrodes–create excess noise

mechanism_principle.content: The symmetric trap design increases the achievable electric field strength at the trap center, making it approximately double that of the previous design.
evidence_spans: the symmetric design means that the achievable electric field strengths at the trap center (for example, for coupling to particle electric dipoles17) are approximately double those possible with our previous design

mechanism_principle.content: Au particles move more slowly because their greater density/inertia makes them decelerate less.
evidence_spans: with the Au particle significantly slower, due to its greater inertia

hypothesis_statement.content: The developed instrumentation and techniques are intended to enable high-stability precision measurements of particles confined in ion traps in high vacuum, and these precision-measurement methods are expected to remain applicable in the ultra-high-vacuum regime.
evidence_spans: We describe below the experimental instrumentation and techniques that we have developed that are optimized for high-stability precision measurements of particles confined in ion traps in high vacuum (10−8 ≤p ≤10−5 Torr).
Although our techniques for precision measurements have been developed and proven at p ≥10−8 Torr, we expect that they will also be applicable in the ultra high vacuum (UHV) regime.

hypothesis_statement.content: Using three phase-locked loops together with thermostatic control should maintain particle amplitudes in the optimal range for measuring motional frequencies and determining Q/M, and this added thermostatic control is intended to remedy the low-amplitude tracking problem in the cooling algorithm.
evidence_spans: In Section VII, we discuss a method for using three phase locked loops (PLLs) to track trapped particle motion along all three axes of confinement. Using these PLL outputs, we implement thermostatic control of particle motion in order to maintain amplitudes that are optimal for measuring motional frequencies and determining Q/M.
To remedy this problem, we have added thermostatic con- trol to our cooling algorithm (Fig. 10).

hypothesis_statement.content: Despite its simplifications, the model should still provide crude but roughly correct estimates of typical particle velocities and stopping distances.
evidence_spans: We nonetheless expect that the model provides crude estimates of typical particle ve- locities and stopping distances that are not too far off.

hypothesis_statement.content: Rapid imaging of thermal motion can provide more extensive characterization of a particle soon after capture.
evidence_spans: To obtain more extensive data on the particle soon after it is collected, we have developed a technique that performs rapid imaging12 on the particle to observe thermal motion in the trap.

hypothesis_statement.content: Low-frequency fluctuations in DC electric fields caused by charge on the trap electrodes are hypothesized to be the primary source of noise, with the largest field magnitudes along the trap z axis.
evidence_spans: These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that low frequency fluctuations in the dc electric fields associated with charge on the trap elec- trodes are the primary source of noise, and that fields along the trap z axis have the largest magnitudes.

hypothesis_statement.content: The particle-transfer technique could be extended to move a particle among multiple specialized traps, each optimized for particular tasks or measurements.
evidence_spans: This technique could in principle be extended to transferring a particle between several traps, each optimized for specific tasks or measurements.

hypothesis_statement.content: Combining these methods with precision rotation and controlled deposition may enable the growth and characterization of new materials in the levitated environment.
evidence_spans: These techniques, in combination with precision rotation17 and controlled deposition of levitated particles32, may also enable the growth and characterization of new materials developed in the levitated environment.

evidence_result.content: Active stabilization and cooling methods enabled long-term trapped-particle stability: the simplest cooling algorithm was sufficient for week-scale stability with 1–10 K center-of-mass temperatures at p ≤ 10^-6 Torr; thermostatic control worked over 10^-8 to 10^-5 Torr with PLLs remaining locked for weeks at the lowest pressures; using these techniques, particle motion could be locked and stabilized for over a month.

metric feedback phase is set for maximum cooling, has proven
adequate for long term stability (>∼weeks), with center of mass
temperatures of 1-10 K at p ≤10−6 Torr.

We
set the values for the band limits to maintain an amplitude
of ∼2 µm for motion along each of the three axes... We
have operated the thermostatic control algorithm successfully
in the range 10−8 ≤p ≤10−5 Torr. At the lowest pressures,
measurements can remain stable–all the PLLs are locked to
the particle motion–for several weeks.

Using these techniques, we have been able to lock and
stabilize particle motion for over a month.

evidence_result.content: After transfer and pumping to high vacuum, particles could remain trapped for up to 24 hours even with feedback and illumination turned off.
evidence_spans: Interestingly, we have found that once a particle has been transferred to an analysis trap and pumped to high vacuum, all feedback control can be interrupted and illumination of the particle entirely turned off for periods of up to 24 hours without particle loss from the trap.

evidence_result.content: Thermal-motion imaging provided insight into non-thermal noise relevant to ion traps exposed to charged particles.

constraint.content: Because Au is highly absorptive, illumination during measurement must be kept very low—well below the level that causes significant heating or evaporation; the paper uses about 1000 W·m−2 at 532 nm.
evidence_spans: Au, like many other materials of interest, is highly absorptive, so our measurements are performed using an illu- mination of only 1000 W·m−2 at 532 nm.
Because Au is highly absorptive, illumination power must be well below that where significant evaporation can oc- cur: we use a 532 nm laser with a power density of ≃1000 W·m−2.

constraint.content: The pinhole aperture between the electrospray emitter and trap chamber must be large enough to avoid clogging and transmit particles, while still keeping the trap-region pressure below about 1 Torr to prevent corona discharge from the high-voltage trap electrodes.
evidence_spans: The inner diameter of the pinhole aperture that separates the electrospray emitter from the trap vacuum chamber should be large enough to avoid clogging and admit as many particles as possible. However, the pressure in the trap region must be lower than ∼1 Torr to prevent corona discharge arising from the high voltages (Vac ≃300 V) on the trap electrodes.

constraint.content: To obtain good thermal-motion spectra for sub-µm particles, measurements should be made at low pressure (about 10–30 mTorr rather than collection pressure near 700 mTorr), with trap frequencies adjusted so the y and z peaks lie below 500 Hz, and in a regime where changing laser power does not affect the data so the particle remains in thermal equilibrium with the background gas.
evidence_spans: While particles are collected at p ∼=700 mTorr, optimal data for spectra for particles of sub-µm dimensions is ob- tained when p =10-30 mTorr... Because Q/M of the particles–and thus their oscillation frequencies–can vary substantially, it is necessary to adjust Ωso that both y and z peaks are found at <500 Hz... Finally, data must be taken in a regime when changes in laser power have no effect on the data, ensuring that the particles are in thermal equilibrium with background gas at T ∼=293 K.
